title: Women Start Out Ahead at Work, but the Childbirth Penalty Grinds the Advantage Away
dek: Right out of college, male and female labour-force participation is nearly identical; ten years later women have fallen behind, and over the next decade or two they partly come back — a curve that lines up closely with the timing of childbirth. What gets ground away is not ability, but continuous accumulation.
why: It takes Goldin's century of empirical work straight into China's retirement ages, maternity-leave coverage and childcare arrangements. More mechanism and concrete numbers than opinion — suited to anyone following the gender income gap and birth policy.
who: Investors, HR people and policy researchers watching the gender income gap, birth policy and workplace issues, plus professional women currently weighing career against childbearing.

points.h: Market competition is a woman's best friend
points.body: Zhao Yaohui relays the economic theory: market competition is the best friend of minorities or women. The logic is that employers initially wanted only single women, but demand for white-collar work rose — once manufacturing scaled up it needed people to keep books, do accounting, sell — work women were better at — so employers were forced to recognise the value of married women who had borne children. Firms that discriminate against women cannot hire when the labour market is tight, get squeezed out, and have no choice but to change their attitudes and practices. She also notes that in the ranking of variables across this century of change, the contraceptive pill probably comes third, because the quiet revolution let women postpone marriage and postpone childbearing to pursue career success.

points.h: Top pay buys you on-call availability
points.body: The childbirth penalty is most obvious in the fifth group of women Goldin identifies. The mechanism is greedy jobs: in recent decades the wage gap has widened, mainly at the top occupations — finance, law, medicine — where incomes keep rising, and the price of that rise is the loss of free time, being summonable at any moment. Because women are the primary carers of children, they cannot walk out when a child runs a fever during a board meeting or falls ill during surgery, so they can only choose fewer of these high-income occupations. The result is that before a child is born a couple's incomes stand in some ratio, and after the birth the distance starts to widen: the husband's wage is unaffected, the wife's income drops, and this loss does not disappear even where welfare is generous — it runs twenty or thirty percent.

points.h: Only unequal pay for equal work counts as discrimination
points.body: Zhao Yaohui first draws the boundary of discrimination: unequal pay for equal work is discrimination, unequal pay for unequal work is not. When women voluntarily choose jobs without overtime or simpler cases for family reasons, the resulting income gap is a childbirth penalty, not discrimination. Real discrimination comes in two kinds — differential treatment in hiring and promotion, and statistical discrimination: an employer predicts that although you have not had a child now, you will in future, that your future labour productivity may be low, and so hires fewer women. She says this kind of discrimination is still quite common at the job-search stage.

points.h: Retiring female associate professors at 55 is discrimination
points.body: Zhao Yaohui names China's most obvious discrimination as lying not in the labour market but in retirement age. Female university teachers who have not been promoted to full professor retire at 55, while men at the same level can go to 60; female workers retire at 50. This stems from regulations of the 1950s, when most work was manual labour and early retirement was a form of labour protection for women. But she says the era is now completely different: the share of manual labour is fairly low, mental work has little to do with age, and the gap between men and women in mental capacity can be considered non-existent, so retiring five years early is utterly unreasonable. The other extreme is rural women, systematically excluded from collective property rights and land compensation — after divorce, neither her husband's family's land nor her natal family's may include her.

points.h: Women's advantage isn't saved up, it slowly leaks away
points.body: Zhao Yaohui uses two cross-sections to illustrate this curve. Goldin found that right after university graduation, male and female employment participation is nearly the same; ten years later women have fallen behind; over the next decade or two they can recover some, but not to where they were — because 996 and constant overtime contribute enormously to individual skill development, and that is precisely the period they are forced to give up. In universities there are many female lecturers, far fewer full professors; in government there are plenty of female section and division chiefs, but at the director-general and minister level they are exceedingly rare. She calls this a process of being filtered out.

points.h: Pronatalist money doesn't reach the opportunity cost
points.body: Why, with the three-child policy, extended maternity leave, parental leave and childcare subsidies appearing so often, has the birth rate still not risen? Zhao Yaohui's explanation is that a large part of the cost of childbearing is indirect cost, opportunity cost, and direct cash payments are a drop in the bucket against the loss of a career. More critical is coverage: the number of female workers with maternity leave is actually very small, not even half, and in a great many firms, among the self-employed, flexibly employed and platform-employed, no one pays maternity insurance for them. So the first priority of policy is to extend maternity leave to all groups, so that during childbearing they have income compensation and can return to their original posts. She also warns that women in the career-promotion window, even with maternity leave, worry that after taking it the position and promotion opportunities will no longer be theirs.

points.h: Later marriage and childbearing shouldn't be encouraged across the board
points.body: Faced with the question of whether later marriage and later childbearing is the better solution, Zhao Yaohui's answer is that it depends on the circumstances. She acknowledges research finding that marrying later means a lower divorce rate — people are more mature, better matched, better at handling relationship problems; but physiologically, childbearing is easier when young and less likely to go wrong, and fertility is best before 30. So the precondition is that the husband must understand and support: among her own colleagues there are many male teachers who, because they took part in childcare, also suffered a lot of the childbirth penalty. If culturally husbands step up and society can provide large numbers of high-quality nurseries, women need not actually postpone very much. Assisted reproduction is a matter of probability; the success rate may reach two-thirds, and some people have tried nine times without success — you cannot count on it as a backstop.

points.h: How a carer treats you depends on whether you have children
points.body: Zhao Yaohui studies the elderly and points out that loneliness in old age is a very serious problem; many older people are depressed, partly from not getting enough social support. People really are quite fragile when old, and neither nursing homes nor nannies can replace the importance of children — when you are ill and hospitalised, the attitude of the carer, and in a nursing home the attitude of the staff, depends to a large extent on whether you have children. She says this may frighten people, but the psychological comfort and sense of security children can bring is still quite important. She adds one more thing: being married without children still does not solve this problem, and the value of children is especially obvious in old age when one is widowed.

terms.def: High-paying occupations that demand constant availability and strip away free time; the main source of the childbirth penalty.
The silent transformation in which the spread of the contraceptive pill let women postpone marriage and childbearing and turn to pursuing careers.
Historical laws barring married women from certain occupations, or requiring them to be dismissed upon marriage.
Employers predicting that a woman will bear children in future and have lower labour productivity, and therefore hiring fewer women.
